title: X86ASM 06: JMP and Functions in Assembly

questions.q: At the machine level, a program's instructions are just a series of bytes in memory with no built-in function boundaries, so the programmer has to create any function structure.
questions.explain: The CPU sees no structure in the instruction bytes. Functions exist only because we arrange jumps and return addresses ourselves.

questions.q: What does putting a label such as `exit:` in front of an instruction actually do?
choices: Names that instruction's memory address so you can refer to it without writing the address out
Turns the instructions that follow into a function with its own scope
Makes the CPU stop when execution reaches the label
Saves a return address automatically when execution reaches it
questions.explain: A label only marks an address, for example 0x401020, so you can refer to it by name. It does not create a function or change how anything runs.

questions.q: If you edit code so that a labeled instruction ends up at a different address, references to that label automatically use the new address.
questions.explain: That is one of the main benefits of labels over hard-coded addresses: the assembler works out the label's address again from the current layout.

questions.q: When straight-line execution reaches a label, the CPU stops there unless something jumps past it.
questions.explain: Labels are not instructions. The instruction pointer keeps going straight down through them, whatever is in the way.

questions.q: What is the only way to change the order in which the CPU executes instructions?
choices: Change the instruction pointer
Add labels to mark where functions begin and end
Leave blank lines between sections of code
Put the address of the next instruction in RAX
questions.explain: The CPU fetches whatever the instruction pointer points to, so changing the flow means changing the instruction pointer. jmp does exactly that.

questions.q: Which x86-64 instruction mnemonic sets the instruction pointer to a target address, such as a label, so execution continues there?
questions.explain: jmp (jump) moves the instruction pointer to the target. For example, `jmp print` skips over any code in between and continues at print.

questions.q: The program was rearranged so the exit code comes before the print code in the source. Why?
choices: Straight-line execution would then exit right away, so a jmp is needed to reach print
The assembler requires exit code to come first
Code placed first runs faster
Labels only work on code near the top of the file
questions.explain: With exit first, the program just quits if run from top to bottom. That makes it necessary to use jmp to get to print.

questions.q: The program starts with `jmp print`. The print code does its write syscall and has no more instructions after it. What happens once the string is printed?
choices: Execution continues into the empty memory after print, and the OS kills the program
Execution automatically goes back to the instruction after `jmp print`
The program exits cleanly with code 0 because the syscall ends it
The CPU loops back to the start of print
questions.explain: Nothing stops execution after the syscall. The instruction pointer keeps going into an empty memory region, and the OS shuts the program down with a segmentation fault.

questions.q: When execution ran past the end of the code into empty memory, the OS shut the program down with what kind of error?
questions.explain: A segmentation fault: the OS forcibly ended the program because it broke the OS's rules by running into memory it should not have.

questions.q: A syscall that writes a string to the screen also ends the program when it finishes.
questions.explain: After the write syscall, execution just continues with the next bytes in memory. Only the exit syscall (rax = 60) ends the program.

questions.q: In the exit sequence `mov rax, 60` / `xor rdi, rdi` / `syscall`, what does `xor rdi, rdi` do?
choices: Sets RDI to 0, so the program exits with code 0
Sets RDI to 60, the exit system call number
Swaps RDI and RAX
Jumps to the address held in RDI
questions.explain: XORing a register with itself always gives 0. RDI holds the exit code, which is why the program exits with code 0.

questions.q: At bottom, every function call works by moving the instruction pointer to the address where the function's code begins.
questions.explain: Jumping the instruction pointer to where you want to run code is the basic mechanism behind any function call.

questions.q: In the first working version, print ends with `jmp exit`. Why is that a rigid design?
choices: print always goes to exit, not back to whatever code called it
jmp can only move forward in memory
jmp exit is slower than a syscall
exit then has to come after print in memory
questions.explain: A proper utility function does one job and then gives control back to its caller, such as main. It should not decide by itself that the program exits.

questions.q: main jumps to the print function on line 6. Once print finishes, which line of main should execution ideally continue on?
questions.explain: The return address is the instruction right after the one that transferred control to the function. Here that is line 7.

questions.q: In the hand-built return mechanism, what does the caller do just before `jmp print`?
choices: Loads R15 with the address of the label where execution should resume
Loads R15 with the address of print
Sets RAX to 60 so print knows to return
Moves the instruction pointer into RDI
questions.explain: The caller and the function agree that R15 holds the return address. The caller puts the address of the resume point (the `return` label) in R15, then jumps to print.

questions.q: With the R15 convention, what single instruction ends print so it goes back to its caller?
questions.explain: `jmp r15` jumps to whatever address the caller stored in R15, so print returns correctly no matter where it was called from.

questions.q: The hardware requires R15 for return addresses. It is the only register jmp can use as a target.
questions.explain: R15 was simply chosen as an agreement between the caller and the function. Any register could have been used for this hand-built convention.

questions.q: What does the R15 return-address approach do better than ending print with `jmp exit`?
choices: print can be called from anywhere in the program
print returns to whatever address the caller put in R15
It supports nested function calls of any depth
It frees R15 for arithmetic
questions.explain: The approach is dynamic: any caller can use print and get control back. It still fails with nested calls, and it ties up R15.

questions.q: With static jumps (print_hello ends with `jmp print_world`, and print_world ends with `jmp exit`), the program still prints hello and world and exits correctly.
questions.explain: The hard-coded chain works, but it is static: each function's next step is fixed instead of returning to whoever called it.

questions.q: main loads R15 with `return` and jumps to print_hello. print_hello loads R15 with `return_hello` and jumps to print_world, which ends with `jmp r15`. When print_hello then runs its own `jmp r15`, where does execution go?
choices: Back to return_hello, because R15 still holds that address
Back to the `return` label in main
Straight to exit
Into empty memory, causing an immediate segmentation fault
questions.explain: print_hello overwrote R15 with return_hello before it called print_world. main's original return address is gone, so nobody remembers where to go back to in main.

questions.q: What word describes accidentally overwriting a register's value before you were done with it, as happened to main's return address in R15?
questions.explain: The value was clobbered: overwritten by accident before it was needed, with no way to get it back.

questions.q: If you used every general-purpose register to hold return addresses, what is the most return addresses you could store at once?
questions.explain: There are 16 general-purpose registers, so 16 is the limit. Recursion can need hundreds or thousands of active calls.

questions.q: Why is storing return addresses in registers, even in all of them, not a workable general solution?
choices: A register holds only one address, so a nested call overwrites the earlier one
If every register held addresses, none would be left for arithmetic or data processing
Recursion can need far more than 16 active return addresses
jmp cannot take its target from a register
Registers are wiped every time a syscall runs
questions.explain: One register is one slot. Using all of them still gives only 16 slots and leaves nothing for computation. jmp r15 worked fine, so registers can be jump targets.

questions.q: How many bytes is one register such as R15, which is also the size of each return-address slot in the stack shown in the lesson?
questions.explain: R15 is a single 8-byte register. The stack is described as 8-byte slots, one after another, like R15 repeated over and over.

questions.q: How does the lesson describe the stack?
choices: A sequence of bytes in memory, split into 8-byte slots, with the current position tracked by the stack pointer
A set of extra hidden CPU registers used only for return addresses
A structure the OS creates only for recursive programs
A special label that marks the end of the program's code
questions.explain: The stack is just memory. Because it can hold many 8-byte return addresses, not just the one that fits in R15, it supports nested function calls.

questions.q: What register keeps track of your current position in the stack?
questions.explain: The stack pointer (RSP on x86-64) tracks where you are in the stack.

questions.q: Which two instructions use the stack to call functions and return from them?
choices: call
ret (return)
jmp
syscall
xor
questions.explain: call and ret (return) use the stack to save and restore return addresses. That replaces the hand-built R15 scheme and supports nested calls.
